Rust is a corrosion product of ferrous metals primarily composed of iron oxides such as magnetite (Fe3O4).
Rust powders were collected from Surabaya, Malang, and Bangkalan regions in Indonesia.
Magnetic separation was performed using a 0.1 Tesla permanent magnet to enrich magnetic ferrite content.
XRF analysis showed iron content of about 82.63 wt% in the rust powder from Surabaya.
XRD confirmed the presence of magnetite phase (Fe3O4) with diffraction peaks at 2θ around 35°.
The rust powders exhibited an amorphous structure with high porosity and low density.
VSM measurements showed saturation magnetization (Ms) of 8.357 emu/g, remanent magnetization (Mr) of 4.535 emu/g, and coercivity (Hc) of 0.0204 T for Surabaya sample.
The rust powders are classified as soft magnetic materials due to low coercivity (<1 T).
Microwave absorption was measured in the X-band frequency range (8-12 GHz) using a Vector Network Analyzer.
Maximum reflection loss (RL) values were -20.15 dB (Surabaya), -12.64 dB (Malang), and -6.75 dB (Bangkalan) at around 11 GHz.
A reflection loss of -20.15 dB corresponds to approximately 99% absorption of incident radar waves.
Magnetic separation improved microwave absorption by increasing the purity of magnetic ferrite particles.
Samples were prepared by milling rust powders and attaching them to 2 mm thick paper molds for VNA testing.
The microwave absorption mechanism involves magnetization of dipoles and conversion of electromagnetic energy into heat via electron vibration.
The absorption bandwidth for Surabaya sample was about 2.51 GHz around the matching frequency.
The study used extraction milling methods to synthesize micro powders of magnetite from corrosion products.
The presence of impurities like Si, Al, Ca, and Ni is normal due to environmental corrosion conditions.
The magnetic powders from Surabaya showed the highest microwave absorption performance among the three locations.
The study suggests that increasing the number of magnetic extraction cycles can further enhance absorption.
Soft magnetic ferrite powders from rust can be used as low-cost, effective radar absorber materials.
